_comment: Carino Offline — the grab list: what to pull down before you can't, in acquisition order. The spine of this file is Miguel's original four-tier post (Fastest / Average / Longest / Wouldn't) and the tiers must keep those ids, that order and those time budgets. BANDWIDTH ASSUMPTION, and every number here depends on it: a 300 Mbit/s sustained link, which is ~135 GB per hour, ~2.25 GB per minute. So `minutes` is roughly `gb / 2.25` — EXCEPT where the link is not the bottleneck. kernel.org, vendor BIOS and driver pages, government law archives, OneDrive, LVFS, hand-picked template sites and anything you have to click through model pickers for are gated by rate limits, pagination, session cookies and human faff; their `minutes` are deliberately larger than their size implies and the item's `note` says so. Local consolidation jobs (own-media) are disk-bound, not link-bound, same idea. The tiers must actually add up to their own labels because the time-budget selector walks items in tier order then `priority`, accumulating `minutes` until the ceiling and dimming the rest: sum(fast) must stay under 60, sum(fast+average) under 180, sum(fast+average+long) under 840. Re-check that arithmetic after every edit or the selector lies to the reader. `tier` must match a tiers[].id and `cat` a cats[].id. Ids are kebab-case, unique, and are the localStorage keys for the checkboxes — renaming one silently unticks it for every existing reader, so append instead of renaming. `gb` is a number and drives every total; `size` is the string shown. The `wont` tier is a decision, not a task: app.js special-cases the id, excludes it from all totals, renders no checkbox, and every entry there must carry a `note` saying what you do instead. Never add a URL you have not opened — a dead link on a page about surviving without the internet is worse than no link. Bump `updated` (YYYY-MM) whenever sizes or commands are re-checked.

tiers.label: Fastest
tiers.blurb: Under an hour for the whole list at 300 Mbit (~2.25 GB/min). Barely any of it is bandwidth — it is small files behind vendor pages, government archives and your own accounts, which is exactly why it goes first.

tiers.label: Average
tiers.blurb: Two more hours at 300 Mbit (~135 GB/h) buys the knowledge core, the translator, the map of the world and the firmware for the things that route your packets. This is where being offline stops being an emergency.

tiers.label: Longest
tiers.blurb: Start it before bed. Even at 300 Mbit a full night is only ~1.5 TB, so everything here is scoped to what actually lands by morning rather than to what you wish you could mirror.

tiers.label: Wouldn't
tiers.blurb: Deliberate non-goals. Written down so the decision is visible and does not get re-litigated at 2 a.m. during a drill.

items.name: Ventoy, installers for all platforms
items.what: One USB stick that boots any ISO you drop onto it, with the Windows, Linux and live-CD installers for making that stick.
items.why: Every other bootable thing on this list becomes a file copy instead of a burn. Take the installers for all three platforms, not just the one you use today — the machine you have to fix may not be yours.
items.get:
# take the .zip (Windows, ~17 MB), the .tar.gz (Linux, ~20 MB) and the
# LiveCD ISO (~196 MB) from the releases page; three files, not one
items.verify: published SHA-256, then boot the stick once before you file it

items.name: Plop Boot Manager
items.what: A tiny boot manager that gives USB boot to machines whose BIOS never had it.
items.why: Two megabytes that resurrect pre-2008 hardware, which is exactly the hardware still working in a rural clinic or a workshop. It costs nothing to hold and cannot be improvised later.
items.note: Keep the floppy and CD images too, not just the Windows loader — the machines that need Plop are the ones with an optical drive and no working USB path.

items.name: Memtest86+
items.what: Bootable memory test, UEFI and legacy images.
items.why: Offline, the fastest way to tell a dying stick of RAM from a software problem you will otherwise chase for two days. Ten megabytes, and it goes on the Ventoy stick you just made.

items.name: Collapse OS
items.what: A self-hosting Forth operating system designed to be built and modified on scavenged 8-bit hardware, with its full documentation.
items.why: The philosophical anchor of this whole list and a real fallback: it assumes the supply chain is gone and targets chips you can still pull out of dead appliances. Take the source, the docs and the tooling, because the point is being able to rebuild it, not run a binary.
items.get:
# clone the repository and keep the generated documentation alongside it;
# the value is the source tree, not a release artifact

items.name: Latest Linux kernel releases, LTS included
items.what: The mainline tarball plus every LTS branch still supported, with the detached signatures.
items.why: The kernel is the one dependency you cannot rebuild from a package mirror if the mirror is stale, and LTS branches are what you will actually be patching on machines that must keep running for years without you.
items.get:
# one tarball plus one .sign per branch; the front page lists which are LTS
curl -LO https://cdn.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/v6.x/linux-<ver>.tar.xz
curl -LO https://cdn.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/v6.x/linux-<ver>.tar.sign
items.verify: unxz then gpg --verify against the kernel.org signing keys you also keep
items.note: Minutes are not transfer time. Choosing which branches, fetching the matching signatures and pulling the signing keys is hand work; the bytes themselves land in well under a minute.

items.name: BIOS/UEFI updates for hardware you own
items.what: The current firmware image and release notes for every board, laptop and server in your possession, filed by vendor and model.
items.why: Vendors delete old firmware without notice and the download pages die before the hardware does. This is the item on the list most likely to be quietly impossible in a year, and it is also the one that unbricks a machine at 3 a.m.
items.get:
# no command exists: every one of these is behind a browser, a model picker
# and often a service tag. Name files <vendor>-<model>-<version>.
items.verify: vendor's published checksum, captured while you can still see the page
items.note: Eight minutes for two gigabytes because the cost is clicking, not downloading. Keep the release notes next to the image — half of BIOS troubleshooting is knowing what a version changed.

items.name: Nvidia / AMD / Intel GPU drivers
items.what: Current and previous-known-good driver packages for all three vendors, Windows first, Linux .run and packaged builds second.
items.why: A machine with no display driver is a machine you cannot use to fix the others. Keeping n-1 matters as much as keeping n: the newest driver is regularly the one that broke the card.
items.note: Grab both the Windows installers and the Linux packages even if you only run one — the Windows box you will be handed to fix is not hypothetical.

items.name: Government public document archive
items.what: The Constitución Política, the federal codes and the full body of vigente federal law as PDFs, from the Cámara de Diputados law library, plus the state-level texts that apply where you live.
items.why: Law is the one reference where the current text and the date of last reform are the whole point, and it is published by an institution whose website is not built to survive anything. Holding it offline is also what lets you answer a contract or licensing question during an outage instead of guessing.
items.get:
# the law library is paginated by ley, one PDF per statute, with a reform
# date per file. A polite recursive fetch with a delay; do not hammer it.
# Record the capture date in the folder name — 'vigente' is a moving target.
items.verify: open the Constitución and check the last-reform date against the index page
items.note: No URL here on purpose: government paths move between administrations and a stale link is worse than none. Minutes are pagination and hand-picking, not bytes.

items.name: Personal documents out of OneDrive
items.what: The whole personal drive pulled to local disk: PDFs of official documents, IDs, certificates, scans and everything else that only exists in somebody else's cloud.
items.why: This is irreplaceable in the strictest sense — not slow to re-fetch, impossible. It is also the single item on this list whose loss is a bureaucratic year of your life rather than a technical inconvenience.
items.get:
# rclone with a Microsoft Graph remote is the reliable path
rclone copy onedrive: ~/offline/onedrive --transfers 4 --checkers 8 --progress
items.verify: rclone check onedrive: against the local copy, then open five random PDFs
items.note: Graph throttles hard on many small files, so eight minutes is realistic even though fifteen gigabytes is under seven at line rate. Encrypt the local copy — this is the folder with your ID scans in it.

items.name: Git bundles of every fleet repo
items.what: One self-contained .bundle per repository, containing all refs and all history.
items.why: A bundle is a single file that clones like a remote. It is the only backup format that survives the forge disappearing, the domain being seized and the disk being read on a machine with no network — all three at once.
items.get:
mkdir -p ~/offline/fleet-bundles
for r in ~/Github/*/; do
  n=$(basename "$r")
  git -C "$r" bundle create ~/offline/fleet-bundles/"$n".bundle --all
done
items.verify: git bundle verify, then clone one on a different machine
items.note: Pair it with a plain rsync of the same tree without .git — the fleet is static and self-hosted, so the copy opens from a filesystem with no build step.

items.name: SSH, GPG and age keys
items.what: Private keys and their trust material for every identity you use to reach your own machines.
items.why: These are the credentials you need most on the day you are locked out of everything convenient, and they are the ones nobody thinks to back up because they have always just been there.
items.get:
tar -czf keys-$(date +%F).tar.gz ~/.ssh ~/.gnupg ~/.config/age
age -p keys-$(date +%F).tar.gz > keys-$(date +%F).tar.gz.age
shred -u keys-$(date +%F).tar.gz
items.verify: decrypt on a second machine and ssh to one host with the restored key

items.name: Password vault and TOTP seeds
items.what: An encrypted export of the vault, plus the TOTP seeds themselves — not just the running authenticator.
items.why: SMS and push 2FA are the first things to fail when transit does. Seeds you hold can be re-enrolled into any authenticator on any device; a phone app you cannot reinstall is a single point of failure with a battery.
items.get:
# Export the vault, then re-encrypt it to a passphrase you can recall
# without a machine. Keep a .kdbx alongside: KeePassXC opens with no server.
age -p vault-export.json > vault-export.json.age
items.verify: open the .age and the .kdbx on an offline machine before you file them
items.note: Print the handful of seeds that gate everything else — the registrar, the hosting account, the bank. Paper does not need a charger.

items.name: The complete RFC archive
items.what: Every RFC, STD, BCP and the index, in text and PDF, from the RFC Editor.
items.why: The best value-per-megabyte item in the entire list. It is the normative source for how the internet actually works — TCP, DNS, HTTP, SMTP, TLS — which is precisely the knowledge you need when you are rebuilding a network by hand with no reference to check against.
items.get:
# the RFC Editor's own rsync host; text is ~555 MB, the PDF set ~1.0 GB
rsync -avz --delete rsync.rfc-editor.org::rfcs-text-only ~/offline/rfc/txt/
rsync -avz --delete rsync.rfc-editor.org::rfcs-pdf-all  ~/offline/rfc/pdf/
items.verify: grep the index for RFC 1918 and open it
items.note: The rfcs / everything-ftp modules pull the whole in-notes tree — tarballs, IENs, JSON, rerendered copies — and are closer to 5 GB. Text plus PDF is the set you actually read.

items.name: NVD / CVE JSON feeds
items.what: The full CVE list and the NVD JSON feeds, one file per year plus the CPE dictionary.
items.why: Offline, you still need to know whether the version you are about to deploy is the one with the hole in it. A local CVE database turns that from a web search into a grep, and it stays useful for years because old CVEs do not stop being true.
items.get:
# yearly JSON archives plus the modified/recent deltas; keep the deltas
# so a monthly refresh is minutes rather than a full re-pull
items.verify: search the local JSON for a CVE you already know the details of
items.note: Rate-limited per IP without an API key, which is why three minutes rather than one. Re-pull the delta feeds monthly while you still can.

items.name: Linux man-pages and POSIX pages
items.what: The upstream man-pages archive, plus the doc subpackages your distribution strips by default.
items.why: A hundred megabytes that restore half of the command line. Minimal container images and trimmed installs routinely ship with no man pages at all, and you discover it the first time you need a flag you half-remember.
items.get:
sudo dnf install man-pages man-db
# and keep the upstream tarball too, for machines you cannot install on
items.verify: man 2 open on a box with the network cable out

items.name: Arch Wiki (.zim)
items.what: The whole Arch Wiki as a single Kiwix ZIM.
items.why: The best practical Linux documentation that exists, and it is almost entirely distribution-agnostic once you ignore pacman. Thirty-odd megabytes that answer systemd, networking, encryption and boot questions on any distro you are actually running — the best value-per-megabyte item on the page after the RFCs.
items.get:
# download.kiwix.org redirects to its load balancer, so let wget span both
wget -c -r -l1 -np -nH -H -D download.kiwix.org,lb.download.kiwix.org \
  --cut-dirs=2 -A 'archlinux_en_all_maxi*.zim' https://download.kiwix.org/zim/other/
items.verify: kiwix-serve and search for systemd-networkd

items.name: Sysinternals Suite
items.what: The full suite as a single zip: Process Explorer, Autoruns, Procmon, PsExec and the rest.
items.why: Fifty megabytes that make a Windows machine diagnosable. Every one of these tools runs portable with no install, which is exactly what you want on a machine you have been handed and are not going to keep.
items.verify: run Autoruns from the extracted folder on a machine with no network

items.name: Wikipedia EN + ES, no images
items.what: The nopic ZIM variants of the English and Spanish editions, served by Kiwix.
items.why: Roughly 40% of the size of the illustrated set for most of the value, and the honest way to get two full editions inside the average tier. Take these first: if the link dies halfway through the maxi download you have nothing, and if it dies halfway through this one you still have Spanish.
items.get:
wget -c -r -l1 -np -nH -H -D download.kiwix.org,lb.download.kiwix.org \
  --cut-dirs=2 -A 'wikipedia_en_all_nopic_*.zim,wikipedia_es_all_nopic_*.zim' \
  https://download.kiwix.org/zim/wikipedia/
items.verify: kiwix-serve --port 8080 *.zim, open an article and follow a link
items.note: Checked 2026-08: en_all_nopic is 49 GB, es_all_nopic 11 GB. A third language is a few gigabytes more for most editions — add it if the tier has room, but check the directory listing rather than assuming a nopic build exists for it. The illustrated versions are a separate item in the Longest tier: English maxi alone is 115 GB.

items.name: Kiwix readers and kiwix-serve
items.what: The desktop apps, the Android APK and the kiwix-tools binaries for every platform you might have to read a ZIM on.
items.why: A library of ZIM files with no reader is a folder of unopenable blobs. Two hundred megabytes buys the guarantee that any phone or laptop on the LAN can open the corpus, including the ones that have never been online.
items.verify: sideload the APK onto a phone in airplane mode and open a ZIM over the LAN

items.name: Wikipedia Medicine (WikiMed)
items.what: The curated medical subset of Wikipedia as a ZIM, in Spanish and English, with images.
items.why: Under three gigabytes, and the one corpus in this list a clinic will actually open during an outage. Disproportionate value per byte for the imaging and clinical side of the practice.
items.get:
# the files are named wikipedia_<lang>_medicine_*, not 'wikimed'
wget -c -r -l1 -np -nH -H -D download.kiwix.org,lb.download.kiwix.org \
  --cut-dirs=2 -A 'wikipedia_en_medicine_maxi_*.zim,wikipedia_es_medicine_maxi_*.zim' \
  https://download.kiwix.org/zim/wikipedia/
items.verify: kiwix-serve and search for a drug you know is in there
items.note: Checked 2026-08: en_medicine_maxi 2.1 GB, es_medicine_maxi 626 MB. MDWiki's own build (mdwiki_en_all_maxi, ~2.1 GB, under /zim/other/) is the other curated medical ZIM if you want a second opinion on the same corpus.

items.name: Wiktionary and Wikivoyage
items.what: Dictionary and travel ZIMs for the same languages you took Wikipedia in.
items.why: A dictionary that works without a network is the difference between reading a foreign document and guessing at it. Wikivoyage is the one that earns its place the day you need to leave.
items.get:
# Wiktionary is published nopic only — there is no maxi build to ask for
wget -c -r -l1 -np -nH -H -D download.kiwix.org,lb.download.kiwix.org \
  --cut-dirs=2 -A 'wiktionary_en_all_nopic_*.zim,wiktionary_es_all_nopic_*.zim' \
  https://download.kiwix.org/zim/wiktionary/
wget -c -r -l1 -np -nH -H -D download.kiwix.org,lb.download.kiwix.org \
  --cut-dirs=2 -A 'wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_*.zim,wikivoyage_es_all_maxi_*.zim' \
  https://download.kiwix.org/zim/wikivoyage/
items.verify: kiwix-serve and look up a word in each
items.note: Checked 2026-08: en Wiktionary is 8.5 GB on its own and es 540 MB; the Wikivoyage pair adds about 1.3 GB. The dictionary is most of this item.

items.name: Argos Translate with language packs
items.what: The offline translation engine plus every language pair you might plausibly need, each one a separate .argosmodel file.
items.why: Machine translation is the capability people assume requires a cloud, and it does not. It runs on a laptop CPU, and it is what makes the ES/EN/JA halves of your own documentation and the fleet's four locales maintainable with no link.
items.get:
pip install argostranslate
# then install each pair from the downloaded .argosmodel files, offline:
# argospm install translate-es_en   (and so on, one per direction)
items.verify: translate a paragraph with the WAN cable out, both directions
items.note: Pairs are directional — es→en and en→es are two files. Pivot pairs through English exist for the rarer languages; take those too or the pair you need will be the missing one.

items.name: Stable Diffusion, offline installer and models
items.what: A local UI that runs without a network, plus a working set of checkpoints, VAEs, LoRAs and upscalers.
items.why: Content generation with no service, no subscription and no terms of use — the checkpoints are the part you cannot re-download once a host takes them down, and hosts take them down regularly.
items.get:
# clone the UI, then fetch checkpoints by file rather than by launcher:
# the launcher's model manager needs a network on first run and the
# weights are the artifact you actually care about
items.verify: generate one image with the machine disconnected, from a cold start
items.note: Hugging Face throttles anonymous pulls, so twenty minutes rather than eighteen. Keep the model hashes: half of these files get re-uploaded under new names and you will want to know which one you had.

items.name: OpenStreetMap extracts, all continents
items.what: The Geofabrik continent-level .osm.pbf extracts covering the whole world, with their md5 files.
items.why: Maps are the offline capability people miss first and assume they cannot have. Continent extracts are the sweet spot: the full planet file is one enormous blob you cannot update incrementally, and country files are a hundred separate downloads to babysit.
items.get:
for c in africa asia australia-oceania central-america europe north-america south-america; do
  wget -c https://download.geofabrik.de/$c-latest.osm.pbf
  wget -c https://download.geofabrik.de/$c-latest.osm.pbf.md5
done
md5sum -c *.md5
items.verify: the published md5 for every file, then open one extract in a viewer
items.note: Checked against Geofabrik's own listing 2026-08: Europe 32.4 GB, North America 17.9 GB, Asia 15.1 GB, Africa 7.4 GB, South America 3.8 GB, Australia-Oceania 1.5 GB, Central America 750 MB — about 79 GB for the set, which is most of a planet file (~80 GB) without being one. Geofabrik rate-limits per IP and will slow you down if you parallelise, so serialise the loop and let it run. Drop Asia and Africa if the tier has to fit something else.

items.name: México extract and a servable basemap
items.what: The country extract at higher priority than the rest of the world, plus a Protomaps or MBTiles basemap so phones on the LAN get actual tiles.
items.why: Raw .pbf is data, not a map — somebody has to render it before it is useful to a person with a phone. This is the item that turns the OSM download into navigation that works in the building.
items.get:
wget -c https://download.geofabrik.de/north-america/mexico-latest.osm.pbf
wget -c https://download.geofabrik.de/north-america/mexico-latest.osm.pbf.md5
md5sum -c mexico-latest.osm.pbf.md5
items.verify: pan the served basemap to your own street on a phone with mobile data off
items.note: The México extract itself is only ~614 MB — the rest of this item is the rendered basemap you build or download from it.

items.name: SystemRescue, Clonezilla and GParted Live
items.what: The three rescue ISOs, dropped onto the Ventoy stick.
items.why: Between them they cover the whole recovery surface: a full toolbox with a network stack, block-level imaging of a dying disk, and partition surgery. Three gigabytes, and every one of them is a download you cannot make from the machine that is broken.
items.get:
# three ISOs from system-rescue.org, clonezilla.org and gparted.org;
# copy straight onto the Ventoy partition
items.verify: boot each one from the stick once, before you need them

items.name: LibreOffice, Firefox ESR, VLC and 7-Zip, offline installers
items.what: Full offline installers — not web stubs — for Windows, plus the Linux packages, in the languages you support.
items.why: These four cover documents, browsing, playback and archives, which is most of what a person actually needs a computer for. The default download for every one of them is a stub that fetches the real payload at install time, and that stub is useless offline.
items.get:
# take the full .msi/.exe offline builds and the langpacks separately;
# Firefox ESR specifically, not rapid release, so it stays valid for a year
items.verify: install each on a VM with no network adapter attached
items.note: Five minutes rather than three because each vendor hides the real offline installer behind a different "other platforms and languages" page.

items.name: fwupd / LVFS firmware cache
items.what: The LVFS metadata plus the cab files for every device fwupd reports on your machines.
items.why: LVFS is the only place firmware updates are packaged in a scriptable, checksummed way instead of a vendor's zip behind a form. Cache the cabs while the service is reachable and fwupd will keep working with the WAN unplugged.
items.get:
fwupdmgr refresh --force
fwupdmgr get-devices
# then pull the cab for each device id and keep them next to the metadata
fwupdmgr download <uri>
items.verify: fwupdmgr local-install <cab> on a device, offline, and check the reported version
items.note: Six minutes for five gigabytes because it is one request per device and the useful set is chosen by hand from what fwupd enumerates.

items.name: OpenWrt images and package feeds
items.what: Factory and sysupgrade images for every router model you own or might buy, plus the matching package feed for each target.
items.why: The router is the piece of infrastructure whose failure takes the whole LAN with it, and stock vendor firmware is the part most likely to have phoned-home dependencies. The package feed matters as much as the image — an OpenWrt box with no feed cannot install so much as a DNS server.
items.get:
# per target: the sysupgrade image, the factory image, and the whole
# packages/ directory for that target and release
items.verify: opkg install from the local feed on a router with no WAN
items.note: Keep the exact release you flashed. Package feeds are pinned to a release and mixing them silently breaks dependencies.

items.name: Meshtastic firmware and apps
items.what: Firmware for each LoRa board you own, the web flasher's offline bundle, and the Android/desktop clients.
items.why: The only communications layer on this list that keeps working when there is no ISP, no cell tower and no power grid to speak of. Half a gigabyte, and flashing it requires the firmware you did not download.
items.get:
# one firmware zip per board variant plus the CLI; the browser flasher
# needs a network, the esptool path does not
items.verify: flash one spare board offline and exchange a message between two nodes

items.name: dcm4che, Orthanc and Weasis
items.what: The DICOM toolkit, the lightweight PACS server and the desktop viewer, with their plugins and installers for every platform.
items.why: This is the working stack of the imaging business, and all three are things you install on a clinic's machine that may have no internet at all. Holding the installers is the difference between a deployment and a return visit.
items.get:
# dcm4che binary zip, Orthanc installers plus the plugin set, Weasis
# installers for Windows/macOS/Linux. Keep the versions that match what
# you already have deployed, not only the newest.
items.verify: send a study from dcm4che storescu into Orthanc and open it in Weasis, all offline
items.note: Pair it with the Carino PACS build so a site can receive studies with nothing but this folder and a laptop.

items.name: Windows 10/11/Server/LTSC English builds
items.what: Current English ISOs for Windows 10, Windows 11, Server and the LTSC editions, with their published hashes.
items.why: You will be handed a Windows machine to fix while offline, and the installer is behind a browser, a licence click and a download page that changes every release. LTSC in particular matters for the clinic and kiosk machines that must not reboot into a feature update.
items.get:
# no command: all of it is browser-gated and licence-gated. Record the
# build number in the filename — 'Windows 11 English' is not a version.
items.verify: published SHA-256, then boot each ISO once in a VM
items.note: Activation is a separate problem with no offline answer. Keep a couple of already-activated VMs snapshotted rather than pretending the ISO solves it.

items.name: Microsoft Update offline files
items.what: The full update payload for the Windows and Office versions you support, fetched with WSUS Offline Update into a folder that patches a machine from USB.
items.why: A freshly installed Windows box with no internet is two hundred missing patches, and Windows Update has no offline path of its own. This is the single item that makes an offline Windows install actually usable rather than nominally installed.
items.get:
# select only the products and languages you support; 'everything'
# multiplies the size several times over for updates you will never apply.
# Run the downloader for one product/language pair at a time (w100 glb),
# then the update generator to build the folder you carry on USB.
items.verify: run the generated installer on a fresh VM with no network and check the build after reboot
items.note: No URL: wsusoffline.net resolved but did not answer on 80 or 443 when last checked (2026-08), so the link is omitted rather than left to rot — find the current distribution point before you rely on this one. Microsoft's CDN throttles bulk fetches, so budget more than the raw arithmetic. Re-run monthly if you can; the delta is small once the first pull is done.

items.name: Snappy Driver Installer Origin, full driverpacks
items.what: SDIO plus the complete driverpack set — network, chipset, storage, audio, printers.
items.why: The classic offline repair deadlock is that the machine needs a network driver and the driver is on the network. Forty-five gigabytes ends that deadlock permanently for almost any Windows machine you will ever be handed.
items.get:
# take the full driverpacks, not the 'lite' network-only set — lite is
# the bootstrap, the full set is the point
items.verify: boot the offline pack on a machine with an unknown NIC and install it
items.note: Torrent is the sane transport for the full set and it is the officially published one.

items.name: Fedora repository, current release, x86_64
items.what: Everything plus updates for the current release, x86_64 only, newest-only, no debuginfo and no source, with metadata regenerated locally.
items.why: Without a package mirror an offline machine stops being maintainable: no security updates, no new tooling, no way to install the thing you need right now. This is the largest single item on the list and it is worth its place.
items.get:
mkdir -p /srv/mirror/fedora
dnf reposync --repoid=fedora --repoid=updates --arch=x86_64 \
  --download-metadata --newest-only --delete -p /srv/mirror/fedora
createrepo_c /srv/mirror/fedora/fedora
items.verify: point a client's baseurl at it and install a package with the WAN out
items.note: Honest caveat: a full Fedora mirror with every release, every arch, sources and debuginfo is well over a terabyte and does not fit in fourteen hours at 300 Mbit. This is one release, one arch, newest builds only — the scope that actually lands by morning. Add n-1 on a second night if you need it.

items.name: EPEL and RPM Fusion packages
items.what: EPEL for the enterprise release you run, plus RPM Fusion free and nonfree for Fedora, x86_64.
items.why: The two repositories that hold the things the base distribution will not ship: codecs, drivers, the long tail of tooling. Missing them offline means discovering that the machine cannot play a video or drive a GPU on the day you need it to.
items.get:
dnf reposync --repoid=epel --repoid=rpmfusion-free --repoid=rpmfusion-nonfree \
  --arch=x86_64 --download-metadata --newest-only --delete -p /srv/mirror/extra
items.verify: install a codec package from the local mirror on a disconnected machine
items.note: Nonfree is a licensing decision, not a technical one — know what you are redistributing before you hand the mirror to a client site.

items.name: RHEL binary DVD and boot ISOs
items.what: Current and n-1 RHEL binary DVDs and boot images, pulled under the developer subscription.
items.why: The enterprise side of the practice runs on RHEL and the ISOs live behind an account login that is exactly the kind of thing that stops working when you need it. The binary DVD also doubles as a local repo, which is what saves a bare-metal install with no network.
items.get:
# portal download, account-gated. Keep the checksum page as a screenshot
# alongside the ISO — the portal will not show it to you offline.
items.verify: published SHA-256, then install once from the DVD with no network configured
items.note: The binary DVD mounted as a local repo installs a usable system with zero network. Test that path before you rely on it.

items.name: Fedora dist-git for the packages you care about
items.what: Clones of the spec files and patch sets from src.fedoraproject.org for the packages you build, maintain or have ever had to patch.
items.why: Binaries let you install; the spec files let you rebuild. When the thing you need has no package for the arch in front of you, a spec and a patch series is the whole difference between recompiling in an afternoon and not shipping at all.
items.get:
# one clone per package; the API paginates and cloning the whole of
# dist-git is tens of thousands of repositories, so pick the list first
fedpkg clone <package>
items.verify: rpmbuild one package from its spec on a machine with no network
items.note: Ten minutes for five gigabytes: this is a per-repository clone loop against a paginated API, not a bulk transfer.

items.name: Install media for the other distributions
items.what: Netinst and live ISOs for Debian, Alpine, Arch and a BSD — install media only, no repositories.
items.why: Being able to install a system is cheap; mirroring its packages is not. Twelve gigabytes of ISOs means you can still bring up a Debian router or an Alpine container host offline, without pretending you can maintain five package archives.
items.get:
# take the full DVD for Debian rather than netinst if you want it to
# install without a mirror; netinst alone is useless with no network
items.verify: published SHA256SUMS, then boot each from the Ventoy stick
items.note: Deliberately paired with the non-goal below: media yes, repositories no. See "Mirroring every other distribution's repositories" in Wouldn't.

items.name: Firmware for every device in the building
items.what: The current firmware image and release notes for every switch, NAS, UPS, printer, BMC and access point you own, filed by vendor and model.
items.why: Vendors delete old firmware without notice and the support pages are the first thing to become unreachable. Anything not covered by LVFS lives here, and this is where the long tail of "the printer needs a firmware to talk to the new TLS" gets solved.
items.get:
# no command: browser, model picker, sometimes a support login.
# <vendor>-<model>-<version>.bin next to <same>-notes.pdf
items.verify: checksum against the vendor's published value while you can still see it
items.note: Twenty minutes for eight gigabytes, and that is optimistic — this is the most tedious item in the whole list and the one with the shortest window before the download page disappears.

items.name: Wikipedia EN + ES with images
items.what: The maxi ZIM variants with illustrations, replacing the nopic set once they verify.
items.why: Images matter more than they sound like they do — anatomy, circuit diagrams, maps, species, mechanisms. This is the largest knowledge item and the one that makes the offline library feel like the real thing rather than a text dump.
items.get:
wget -c -r -l1 -np -nH -H -D download.kiwix.org,lb.download.kiwix.org \
  --cut-dirs=2 -A 'wikipedia_en_all_maxi_*.zim,wikipedia_es_all_maxi_*.zim' \
  https://download.kiwix.org/zim/wikipedia/
items.verify: kiwix-serve, open an article with photographs, then delete the nopic set
items.note: Checked 2026-08: en_all_maxi is 115 GB and es_all_maxi 38 GB — that is the real number, and it is why the nopic set goes in the earlier tier. Keep nopic until maxi verifies: two partial copies is a waste, zero copies for an hour is a risk.

items.name: Stack Exchange network dumps
items.what: Stack Overflow plus Server Fault, Super User, Unix & Linux and the other sites you actually read, as ZIMs.
items.why: The programming and sysadmin lifeline. Almost every non-trivial error message you will hit offline has already been answered here, and nothing else on this list substitutes for it.
items.get:
wget -c -r -l1 -np -nH -H -D download.kiwix.org,lb.download.kiwix.org \
  --cut-dirs=2 -A 'stackoverflow.com_en_all_*.zim,serverfault.com_en_all_*.zim,unix.stackexchange.com_en_all_*.zim' \
  https://download.kiwix.org/zim/stack_exchange/
items.verify: paste a real error message into kiwix-serve's search and get the answer you remember
items.note: Checked 2026-08: Stack Overflow is 75 GB and is the whole item — Server Fault (1.5 GB) and Unix and Linux (1.2 GB) are rounding. The Stack Overflow ZIM is also rebuilt rarely; the newest is a 2023 snapshot, which is fine for solved problems and useless for anything current.

items.name: Project Gutenberg
items.what: Spanish Gutenberg complete, plus the English library by Library of Congress class rather than in one piece: literature, medicine and technology.
items.why: Public domain means it is unambiguously yours to hold, copy and hand out on a disc, which makes it the backbone of anything you press and give away. It is also the only large media collection on this list with no licensing asterisk.
items.get:
# es_all is small enough to take whole; en_all is not (see the note)
wget -c -r -l1 -np -nH -H -D download.kiwix.org,lb.download.kiwix.org \
  --cut-dirs=2 -A 'gutenberg_es_all_*.zim,gutenberg_en_lcc-pr_*.zim,gutenberg_en_lcc-ps_*.zim,gutenberg_en_lcc-r_*.zim,gutenberg_en_lcc-t_*.zim' \
  https://download.kiwix.org/zim/gutenberg/
items.verify: open three books on a phone with mobile data off
items.note: Scoped deliberately. Checked 2026-08: gutenberg_en_all is 206 GB, which is a night on its own and would push this tier past its own budget, so this takes the per-class builds instead — English literature (lcc-pr, 15 GB), American literature (lcc-ps, 15 GB), medicine (lcc-r, 1.9 GB), technology (lcc-t, 12 GB) — plus all of Spanish (1.7 GB). Add lcc-pz (juvenile, 18 GB) or lcc-q (science, 17 GB) on a second night.

items.name: DevDocs docsets
items.what: Self-hosted DevDocs with the doc sets for the languages, frameworks and tools you actually write.
items.why: Losing documentation is what makes an offline developer stop being a developer. A couple of gigabytes buys back the reference half of the job, and its search is better than most vendors' own.
items.get:
git clone https://github.com/freeCodeCamp/devdocs
cd devdocs && bundle install
# naming the sets you use is a fraction of --all and takes a fraction as long
thor docs:download <doc> <doc> <doc>
# Kiwix also publishes one ZIM per docset under
# https://download.kiwix.org/zim/devdocs/ if you would rather not run Ruby
items.verify: search a symbol you use weekly with the WAN unplugged
items.note: Ten minutes for two gigabytes because the downloader scrapes set by set and is polite about it, not because the bytes are slow. Individual docsets are tens of megabytes — Qt and scikit-learn, two of the largest, are about 50 MB each — so a personal selection is small and the whole of DevDocs is single-digit gigabytes.

items.name: Kolibri education channels
items.what: Khan Academy and the other channels relevant to the people who will actually use them, imported into a local Kolibri server.
items.why: The clearest client-facing offering in the whole plan: a school or clinic with no usable link gets a curriculum server for the price of a mini PC. Optional for you, load-bearing for the commercial case.
items.get:
kolibri manage importchannel network <channel_id>
kolibri manage importcontent network <channel_id>
items.verify: complete one exercise on a client device with the WAN out

items.name: Lurk and save the sites you rely on
items.what: Full snapshots — HTML, PDF, screenshot, WARC — of every page in your bookmark seed list, taken with ArchiveBox or wget --mirror.
items.why: The pages you rely on are not a set you can reconstruct; you only notice one is gone when you reach for it. This is also the only item here that preserves pages which will simply cease to exist rather than merely become unreachable.
items.get:
# flatten the browser's bookmark export to one URL per line first
grep -oE 'https?://[^"]+' bookmarks.html | sort -u > seeds.txt
docker run -v $PWD:/data -it archivebox/archivebox init --setup
docker run -v $PWD:/data -it archivebox/archivebox add < seeds.txt
items.verify: open a snapshot of a page you know has since changed
items.note: Minutes are dominated by headless rendering, one page at a time — this is CPU-bound, not link-bound, and it will not go faster on a better connection. Schedule it monthly or it will be six months stale the day you need it.

items.name: HTML/CSS templates and component sources
items.what: Saved copies of the layouts, component patterns and CSS you build from, kept as working files rather than as links in a bookmark folder.
items.why: Building a site offline with no reference means reinventing every layout by hand. A folder of known-good markup is the difference between shipping a client's page in an afternoon and rediscovering flexbox from first principles.
items.get:
# per-site, by hand: save the page complete, keep the CSS, note the licence
# in a LICENCE file next to it or you will not remember what you may reuse
items.verify: open one template from the filesystem with the network off and confirm nothing 404s
items.note: Twelve minutes for five gigabytes because this is entirely hand-curated. Record each template's licence as you save it — reusing something you cannot relicense is a problem you inherit years later.

items.name: Open-weight model files
items.what: The largest instruct model that fits in VRAM with room for context, plus a smaller CPU-runnable fallback and an embedding model for RAG over your own documents.
items.why: The offline oracle. A local model that has read your own documentation covers the questions no ZIM answers, and the weights are the part you cannot re-download later if the host pulls them.
items.get:
ollama pull <model>
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
# archive ~/.ollama/models itself — the blobs are the artifact, and the
# tag may not resolve next year
items.verify: ask it something answerable only from your own RAG corpus, disconnected
items.note: Take the smaller fallback too. A model that needs a GPU you no longer have is not an offline capability.

items.name: Container images, pull-through cache warmed
items.what: A registry running in proxy mode, warmed by pulling every image your compose files actually name, plus docker save tarballs of the handful that must come back first.
items.why: A pull-through cache holds exactly the images you have used, which is the set you will need again. It is also what lets a container host that has lost its link still restart a service after a power cut.
items.get:
docker run -d --restart=always -p 5000:5000 --name registry-mirror \
  -e REGISTRY_PROXY_REMOTEURL=https://registry-1.docker.io registry:2
# then warm it by pulling through it, and docker save the three you cannot
# afford to have miss: the reverse proxy, the DNS server, the CA
items.verify: cut the WAN, then docker compose down && up on one stack

items.name: PyPI pull-through, warmed
items.what: devpi in front of PyPI, caching on demand, warmed by installing every requirements file you own through it.
items.why: A full PyPI copy is enormous and mostly packages you will never import. The pull-through holds your actual dependency closure, which is both smaller and more useful — and pip install offline is otherwise a hard stop.
items.get:
pip install devpi-server devpi-client
devpi-init && devpi-server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 3141
# pip config set global.index-url http://<host>:3141/root/pypi/+simple/
# then: pip download -r requirements.txt for every project you own
items.verify: pip install a cached package with the WAN unplugged
items.note: Warming is per-project and serial, so the minutes are the loop, not the bytes.

items.name: npm pull-through, warmed
items.what: Verdaccio as the registry for every project on the LAN, warmed by running npm ci in each of them once.
items.why: node_modules is the classic thing that cannot be reconstructed offline. The fleet is vendored and needs almost none of this, but anything with a build step does, and a cold cache is the same as no cache.
items.get:
npm i -g verdaccio && verdaccio
# npm config set registry http://<host>:4873/
# then npm ci in every project so the cache holds the real closure
items.verify: npm ci in a cached project with the WAN unplugged

items.name: Flatpak sideload repository
items.what: A self-contained sideload repo of the desktop applications you deploy, built with flatpak create-usb.
items.why: create-usb produces a directory any machine can install from with no ostree incantations and no remote configured. It is the practical way to hand a full desktop application to a machine that has never been online.
items.get:
flatpak create-usb /srv/mirror/flatpak \
  org.blender.Blender org.kde.krita org.inkscape.Inkscape org.freecad.FreeCAD
items.verify: install one app from the repo on an offline machine and launch it
items.note: Runtimes are the bulk of it and they are shared — adding the fifth app costs far less than the first. The four named here plus their GNOME and KDE runtimes are only a few gigabytes; ten is the room to add the rest of a desktop, not the cost of these.

items.name: ffmpeg static builds
items.what: Statically linked ffmpeg binaries for Linux, Windows and macOS, plus the source tarball.
items.why: One binary, no dependencies, and it converts or repairs essentially any media file you will ever be handed. The static build in particular runs on distributions whose package manager you cannot reach.
items.get:
# take the static builds for each platform plus the release tarball,
# so you can rebuild it if the binary does not match the libc in front of you
items.verify: transcode a file with the binary on a machine with nothing else installed

items.name: PrusaSlicer, printer firmware and a model library
items.what: The slicer with its full profile bundle, the firmware for each printer you own, and a mirror of the model collections you actually print from.
items.why: A 3D printer is the closest thing on this list to a local supply chain — brackets, clips, housings, replacement knobs for hardware nobody stocks any more. Slicer profiles and printer firmware are also small files that vanish from vendor sites between revisions.
items.get:
# slicer AppImage/installer plus the vendor profile bundle, the firmware
# .hex/.bbf per printer, then the models one collection at a time
items.verify: slice a model and print it with the machine's network disconnected
items.note: Model libraries are per-file downloads with licences attached — keep the licence with the STL. Fifteen minutes is the clicking, not the transfer.

items.name: DICOM test datasets and standard documents
items.what: Public sample studies across modalities, plus the DICOM standard parts as PDFs and the conformance statements for the equipment you support.
items.why: You cannot debug a PACS integration with no studies to send, and the standard itself is the reference that settles every argument about what a tag means. Both are free to hold and impossible to improvise.
items.get:
# sample studies per modality — CT, MR, US, CR, mammo — plus every
# published part of the standard as PDF, and the vendor conformance
# statements for the scanners you actually integrate with
items.verify: send one study through your own PACS end to end, offline
items.note: Sample data must be genuinely public and de-identified. Never keep patient studies in an archive like this — that is a different legal universe.

items.name: Consolidate your own photos and video
items.what: Every phone backup, camera card and scattered drive pulled into one authoritative tree, then a first snapshot of it.
items.why: The only content on this list that no mirror anywhere can replace, and almost always the least organised. Get one copy under backup before you get a tidy one.
items.get:
rsync -aHAX --info=progress2 /mnt/phone-backups/ /srv/media/photos/
restic -r /srv/backup init
restic -r /srv/backup backup /srv/media
items.verify: restore one file to /tmp and open it — a backup you have not restored is a rumour
items.note: The only item here that is not a download: this is a local disk-to-disk copy at roughly 110 MB/s, so the minutes come from spindle and USB speed, not from the 300 Mbit link — the same 200 GB over the wire would be an hour and a half. It runs in parallel with everything else on this page.

items.name: Licences, invoices, serials and warranties
items.what: Scans of purchase records, licence keys, service tags and support contacts for every piece of hardware in the building, OCR'd and indexed.
items.why: An RMA needs shipping and internet, so the warranty is worth little offline — but the serial numbers, model revisions and firmware versions are what let you buy the right spare part or diagnose the wrong one.
items.get: cp ~/scans/*.pdf /srv/paperless/consume/
items.verify: full-text search for one serial number and get the right document back
items.note: The scanning is the slow part and it is entirely offline work — nothing here touches the link at all.

items.name: Contacts and calendar export
items.what: vCard and ICS files for every address book and calendar you actually use.
items.why: Phone numbers are the fallback channel when everything else is down, and they live in exactly one place that belongs to somebody else.
items.get:
# every provider still has a working export today; use it today.
# Contacts -> Export vCard, Calendar -> Export ICS.
items.verify: import the vCard into a second client and count the entries
items.note: Print the ten numbers you would call in an actual emergency. A vCard on a dead phone is not a contact list.

items.name: Internal CA root and intermediate
items.what: The whole CA state directory: root key, intermediate, provisioners and the ACME configuration.
items.why: If you cannot reach a public ACME service, the internal CA is the only thing still issuing certificates. Losing its root means redistributing trust to every device in the building by hand.
items.get:
tar -czf step-ca-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C ~/.step .
age -p step-ca-$(date +%F).tar.gz > step-ca-$(date +%F).tar.gz.age
shred -u step-ca-$(date +%F).tar.gz
items.verify: restore to a scratch directory and issue one test certificate from it

items.name: DNS zone export and registrar record
items.what: The full zone in BIND text form, plus a printout of the registrar's record set and the account recovery details.
items.why: Rebuilding a zone from memory is a day of work and you will get a record wrong. If the domain is suspended you still need to know exactly what it said, to reproduce it on internal names.
items.get:
# the DNS server's own export is safer than AXFR if you have it
dig AXFR carino.systems @<authoritative-ip> > carino.systems.zone
items.verify: grep for the apex, MX, and every subdomain you actually serve

items.name: Printed emergency runbook and IP card
items.what: Two sides of paper: internal IP plan, service ports, the boot order for a cold start, and who to call. Laminated, one copy per site.
items.why: Every digital copy of the runbook lives behind something the runbook exists to fix. Paper has no dependency graph, and writing it is what exposes the steps you had only ever done from muscle memory.
items.verify: hand it to someone who has never touched the rack and watch them boot it
items.note: Reprint on any renumbering. A card with a stale IP is worse than no card, because it will be believed. Fifteen minutes of writing, zero bytes.

items.name: Copyrighted media
items.what: Films, series, music and the rest of a commercial media library, hoarded ahead of a shutdown.
items.why: The internet going down does not mean media distribution falls with it. CDs, DVDs, Blu-rays, vinyl and every other offline format still exist and still work, and since USB storage and hard drives keep working too, you can simply pay for digital copies and hold the files. The same goes for games. Deeper changes would follow, but that is a different subject.
items.note: Instead: buy DRM-free — GOG for games, direct downloads for music and film — own the actual files, and press your own discs for anything you want to hand to someone. The Sneakernet section is this argument built out: physical distribution is a working channel, not a fallback.

items.name: Pre-downloading DRM'd game libraries
items.what: Filling a disk with a Steam or launcher library ahead of time, on the assumption offline mode will carry it.
items.why: Offline mode on every major launcher re-authorises on a schedule you do not control, and a pre-downloaded library that refuses to launch during a blackout is worse than knowing you never had it. You are storing hundreds of gigabytes of licence, not of game.
items.note: Instead: buy DRM-free and keep the installers as files. If you do play launcher titles, treat them as best-effort entertainment, never as something the plan depends on.

items.name: Mirroring every other distribution's repositories
items.what: Full package archives for Arch, Debian, Slackware, Gentoo and the BSDs alongside the RHEL/Fedora mirror.
items.why: Realistically there is not time. Each one is hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes, they all go stale at different rates, and a night is a night — so the choice is a deep, current RHEL/Fedora mirror or five shallow stale ones. Fedora is what the machines here run, so Fedora is what gets mirrored properly.
items.note: Instead: keep their install media, which is twelve gigabytes and covers bringing a system up — see "Install media for the other distributions" in the Longest tier. Debian's full DVD in particular installs a usable system with no mirror at all.

items.name: Full PyPI, npm and Docker Hub mirrors
items.what: Complete copies of the public language and container registries rather than caches of what you use.
items.why: All three are unbounded, grow hourly and are stale the day the copy finishes. The hit rate on the parts you will actually install is a rounding error against the disk they cost, and a mirror with no completion criterion is a job that never ends.
items.note: Instead: run the pull-through caches in the Longest tier and warm them deliberately, so the cache holds exactly your dependency closure. Then docker save the three images that must come back first after a cold start.

items.name: A second copy in someone else's cloud
items.what: Treating a cloud backup provider as the offsite half of the 3-2-1 rule.
items.why: Cloud backup is the one countermeasure that fails in every scenario this plan is about. If transit, DNS or the account itself is what broke, the offsite copy is exactly as unreachable as the thing it was insuring — and it is the copy you would be reaching for at precisely that moment.
items.note: Instead: a second physical site replicated over an overlay network, plus cold drives rotated by hand. The offsite copy has to be one you can drive to.
